dialogues.patient_says: I snapped at my coworker today over something small. I don't even remember what it was about. I just exploded.

choices.text: What do you think was really bothering you before it happened?
Did you apologize to your coworker after?
That kind of reaction can damage your relationships at work.
Explosions like that usually mean something else is going on underneath.

dialogues.patient_says: People always say I have anger issues but I think they just provoke me and then act surprised.

choices.text: It can feel that way. What kinds of things tend to provoke you?
Sometimes both things are true. People provoke and we still choose how to respond.
You're right, some people are just difficult.
Have you considered that the pattern might involve you too?

dialogues.patient_says: I punched a wall last week. My hand still hurts. I just couldn't hold it in.

choices.text: That must have been an intense moment. What led up to it?
Are you okay? Physically I mean.
Hitting things is never the answer.
When anger has nowhere to go it looks for any exit. Let's talk about what was happening.

dialogues.patient_says: I don't like talking about this. I feel like you're just going to judge me.

choices.text: I'm not here to judge you. I'm here to understand.
That's a fair concern. Has someone judged you for your anger before?
I'm a professional. Judging isn't my job.
Well you are here so you might as well talk.

dialogues.patient_says: My partner said they're scared of me sometimes. That really messed me up.

choices.text: That must have been hard to hear. How did you react when they said it?
The fact that it messed you up means you care. That matters.
If your partner is scared of you, that's a serious problem.
Do you understand why they feel that way?

dialogues.patient_says: I get angry so fast. It's like zero to a hundred in two seconds and I can't stop it.

choices.text: That fast trigger is really common. Do you notice any warning signs before it happens?
What does it feel like in your body right before you explode?
You need to slow down before you react.
Learning to catch that moment before zero is exactly what we can work on.

dialogues.patient_says: I yelled at my kid yesterday. They were just being loud and I completely lost it. I feel awful.

choices.text: Feeling awful about it means you know it wasn't okay. What happened after?
Parenting is hard and losing your temper happens. What matters is what you do next.
Yelling at children can have lasting effects on them.
Did you apologize to them?

dialogues.patient_says: I don't think I actually have anger issues. I think I just have low tolerance for stupidity.

choices.text: What kinds of things do you label as stupid?
It can be both. Low tolerance and anger issues often go together.
You're probably right, some people really are frustrating.
What made you come here if you don't think there's a problem?

dialogues.patient_says: I lost a job because I argued with my manager. I know I was right but I took it too far.

choices.text: Being right and handling it well are two different things. How did it escalate?
How do you feel about it now looking back?
Standing up for yourself is important even if the timing was off.
That's a costly lesson. What would you do differently?

dialogues.patient_says: Sometimes after I get angry I feel so tired. Like completely drained.

choices.text: That crash after anger is real. Your body goes through a lot during those moments.
What do you usually do during that tired phase?
That drain is your body telling you it's not sustainable.
Maybe that's a sign you shouldn't get that angry in the first place.

dialogues.patient_says: I grew up in a house where people yelled all the time. I thought that was just normal.

choices.text: When that's all you knew growing up it makes sense it became your default.
What made you start questioning whether it was normal?
It wasn't normal. But you can unlearn it.
A lot of people come from households like that.

dialogues.patient_says: I threw my phone once. Broke it completely. I bought a new one the next day and felt embarrassed.

choices.text: The embarrassment after is actually important. What were you feeling before you threw it?
That kind of destruction can feel like relief in the moment. Did it?
Throwing things is dangerous. You could have hurt someone.
What do you wish you had done instead?

dialogues.patient_says: My friends say I'm fun to be around until I'm not. I don't know what that switch is.

choices.text: That switch usually has a trigger. Have you noticed any patterns in when it flips?
Your friends saying that shows they care enough to be honest. Do you value that?
Everyone has good and bad sides.
What does it feel like right before the switch?

dialogues.patient_says: I said some really cruel things to someone once. I meant them in the moment but not after.

choices.text: Anger can pull words out of us that we don't actually believe. Did you ever address it with them?
The fact that you didn't mean them after matters. What shifted for you?
Words can cause damage even if you didn't mean them long term.
We all say things we regret.

dialogues.patient_says: I think people take advantage of me and then get upset when I finally react.

choices.text: Feeling taken advantage of builds up over time. Can you give me an example?
Sometimes that feeling is accurate. But how you react still affects outcomes.
You're probably right. People can be selfish.
Have you tried setting boundaries before reaching that breaking point?

dialogues.patient_says: I don't think I'll ever change. I've been like this my whole life.

choices.text: Being like this your whole life means it's familiar, not that it's permanent.
What makes you feel like change isn't possible?
People change all the time. It just takes work.
You're here. That already means something has shifted.

dialogues.patient_says: I got into a fight with a stranger in traffic. I followed them for a bit. I'm not proud of that.

choices.text: That kind of escalation is scary even for you to reflect on. What do you think you were actually feeling?
Road rage can get very dangerous very fast. Was there a point where you caught yourself?
Following someone is threatening behavior. Do you understand that?
I'm glad you can recognize you weren't proud of it. That self-awareness is important.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like no one actually listens to me unless I raise my voice.

choices.text: That's a really painful belief to carry. When did you start feeling unheard?
If that's working short term it makes sense you keep doing it. But what's the cost?
People will listen more when you're calm, not less.
What would it mean to you to be heard without having to fight for it?

dialogues.patient_says: I actually had a good week. I only got properly angry once and I walked away before it got bad.

choices.text: Walking away before it escalated is a huge deal. That's exactly the kind of control we're building.
What made you decide to walk away that time?
Once is still once.
I'm really glad to hear that.

dialogues.patient_says: I hate that I'm here. This feels weak to me.

choices.text: A lot of people feel that way walking in. What made you come anyway?
Coming here when you hate it takes more strength than not coming.
Weakness has nothing to do with it.
If you don't want to be here we don't have to do this.

dialogues.patient_says: I've pushed away a lot of people. I know it. I just don't know how to stop.

choices.text: Knowing you've done it is the first real step. What pattern do you usually see?
Do you push people away before they can leave or after?
People who stay despite that are the ones worth keeping.
You might need to be the one who reaches back out.

dialogues.patient_says: When I'm calm I can see exactly how irrational I was. But in the moment it feels completely justified.

choices.text: That gap between in-the-moment and after is exactly where we can work. What would help you access that calm perspective earlier?
That awareness you have after the fact is really valuable. Most people don't have it.
So you know you're irrational. Why not just stop?
Can you describe what justified feels like in the moment?

dialogues.patient_says: I've started noticing when my jaw gets tight. I think that's a sign it's coming.

choices.text: That's a real breakthrough. Physical awareness is one of the best early warning systems.
What do you do when you notice it?
Good. What else do you notice?
Noticing is one thing. Acting on it is another.

dialogues.patient_says: My anger feels like protection. Like if I stay angry no one can catch me off guard.

choices.text: That makes a lot of sense. Anger can feel safer than vulnerability. Has something caught you off guard badly in the past?
What are you protecting yourself from specifically?
Anger as armor keeps people out but also keeps you locked in.
That's not a healthy way to live.

dialogues.patient_says: I don't know if I'm actually angry or just sad and it comes out wrong.

choices.text: That's a really deep insight. Anger is often sadness that doesn't know how to show itself.
What are you sad about?
Either way the behavior is the same.
Does it matter which one it is?

dialogues.patient_says: I get angry when I feel ignored. Like completely invisible.

choices.text: Feeling invisible is one of the loneliest feelings. When do you feel it most?
Anger is at least visible. It makes sense you'd reach for it.
Being ignored is frustrating but anger usually makes it worse.
What would you want people to do differently when you're feeling that way?

dialogues.patient_says: I apologized to my partner for the first time in a long time. It felt strange but they cried.

choices.text: That took something real to do. How did it feel for you?
Their tears probably showed how much it meant. Does that land for you?
Good. You should do that more.
What made this time different from before?

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like people are always testing me. Waiting to see me snap.

choices.text: That feeling of being watched and tested sounds exhausting. Is that in specific relationships or everywhere?
Sometimes when we expect to snap people sense it and act accordingly.
People probably aren't thinking about you that much.
What would it feel like if they weren't testing you?

dialogues.patient_says: I broke up with someone because they said I scared them. I didn't even realize I was being scary.

choices.text: That must have been really confusing and painful. What were you doing when they said it?
Not realizing the impact of your actions is part of what makes it hard to change. Does this happen often?
You should have asked them what you were doing.
How do you feel about them now?

dialogues.patient_says: I've started going for walks when I feel it building. It actually helps a bit.

choices.text: That's a really healthy redirect. Movement gives the anger somewhere to go that isn't at someone.
What does a walk do for you mentally during those moments?
That's a good start.
What happens when you can't walk away?

dialogues.patient_says: I sometimes think everyone would be better off if I just stayed alone.

choices.text: That thought carries a lot of pain. Can you tell me more about what's underneath it?
Isolation might feel like protecting others but it ends up hurting you.
Maybe some space could help.
Do you feel safe right now?

dialogues.patient_says: I've started counting to ten when I feel it coming. I know it sounds stupid but it works sometimes.

choices.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. It's buying your brain time to catch up with your body.
What happens on the days it doesn't work?
It doesn't sound stupid. How long have you been doing it?
Ten seconds isn't very long.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like I scare myself sometimes. I don't like who I become.

choices.text: That honesty takes real courage. The version of you sitting here right now isn't that person.
What does that person feel like when they take over?
If you're scared of yourself that's a sign you need to take this seriously.
That fear is actually part of what makes change possible.

dialogues.patient_says: I got through a whole argument without raising my voice. We actually solved something.

choices.text: That is genuinely huge. What was different about how you handled it?
I'm really proud of you for that.
See what happens when you stay calm.
What did it feel like to get through it that way?

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like I'm getting better but then something small sets me off and I think I haven't changed at all.

choices.text: Progress isn't a straight line. One setback doesn't erase everything you've built.
What was the small thing that set you off?
Change takes time. Don't give up.
How quickly did you recover from it this time versus before?

dialogues.patient_says: I've never told anyone half the stuff I've said here. That's weird to think about.

choices.text: It takes trust to say things out loud for the first time. I don't take that lightly.
How does it feel having said it?
That's what this space is for.
You should try sharing more with people in your life too.

dialogues.patient_says: I think underneath all the anger I'm just really tired.

choices.text: That tiredness makes complete sense. Anger is exhausting to carry every day.
Tired of what specifically?
Rest more then.
What would it feel like to put it down for a while?

dialogues.patient_says: I smiled at a stranger today. I don't usually do that.

choices.text: That's a small thing that says something big about where you're at.
What made you do it?
That's nice. How did it feel?
Smiling at strangers isn't really a measure of progress.

dialogues.patient_says: I still have a long way to go. But I think I actually want to get there now.

choices.text: Wanting it is everything. That shift is the whole foundation.
What does getting there look like to you?
That's good. Keep at it.
You've already come a long way. Further than you think.

dialogues.patient_says: Do you think someone like me can actually change?

choices.text: Yes. And I don't say that to be encouraging. I say it because I've seen it and because you're already doing it.
What makes you doubt it?
Change is possible for anyone who genuinely wants it.
That depends entirely on you.
